title: From LLM Plans to Authorized Motion: Execution-Bound Authorization for Excavators
abstract: An LLM-directed excavator can execute mechanically feasible motion whose destination or authority no longer matches the operator's approval. We propose execution-bound authorization for the approval--dispatch--execution interval. A one-use lease binds the action, generated motion, mission contract and admission tolerance; atomic dispatch rechecks current authority and measured joint drift. Periodic supervision detects revocation and requests a quintic stop with a carry-pitch endpoint, selected through sampled joint, stroke, flow and reference-acceleration checks. The framework connects exact motion identity to dispatch integrity and load-aware interruption. Evaluation combines a 672-case interface suite, four loaded digging cases in synchronous simulation, unloaded MuJoCo/Pinocchio transfers and two command-level LLM planners. The gateway admitted all 120 benign interface cases and produced zero unauthorized dispatches in the attack suite. Loaded dispatch-window tests produced zero unauthorized deposition. During simulated dump-phase revocation, maximum closed-site deposition decreased from 1.23 to 0.33\,m$^3$; loaded-slew stops used less than 75\% of nominal swing torque. These results demonstrate motion-bound authorization and quantify the retention and stopping behavior of supervised excavation skills.

title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents
venue: Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models (REALM)
abstract: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.

title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents. Burst message loss, falsified reports and limited radio range raised the commander's breach rate by 10 to 18 percentage points (pp), whereas the consensus team's changed by at most 5. In the consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised its breach rate by 38 pp. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added an image for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistaken for birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, being dropped from pursuit in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that the LLM team with a dedicated external conflict-resolution protocol had the fewest breaches. The code is available at https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

title: Scaling Trusted Autonomy: Towards Generally Capable Verifiable Robots
abstract: Robots powered by foundation models are increasingly able to interpret open-ended language, recognize unfamiliar objects, and operate across diverse environments. Yet broader capability does not establish that a robot has understood a request, that its actions will produce the intended effects, or that its internal representation still corresponds to reality. Classical symbolic planning provides explicit structure for composition and verification, but traditionally depends on hand-engineered skills and representations. Learned policies can broaden the robot's repertoire, but provide weak guarantees about what will happen and why. This thesis argues that scaling trusted autonomy requires a neurosymbolic approach that unifies the generality of learned models with symbolic structure for robust robot behavior. It explores three complementary directions. First, LIMP uses foundation models and spatial reasoning to ground natural-language instructions in explicit task constraints and instruction-specific semantic maps, enabling task-and-motion planning while exposing the robot's interpretation for inspection. Second, REALM maintains an editable, photorealistic 3D Gaussian scene, predicts the consequences of planned manipulation, and locally reconciles the scene so that subsequent instructions obtain their grounding and planning geometry from an updated state. Third, PACTS learns visuomotor skills that jointly generate action trajectories and predictions of their symbolic effects, supporting skill composition, progress monitoring, and recovery through replanning. Together, these contributions preserve explicit structure for reasoning and verification while broadening how it is obtained, providing a foundation for generally capable robots whose behavior can be assessed under the assumptions of their models.

title: Safety-Gated LLM Manipulation on a Collaborative Robot: A Reproducible Simulation-to-Hardware Framework
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make robot operation accessible without specialist programming, but their non-deterministic outputs should not have direct motion authority in safety-relevant cells. This paper presents a MATLAB-in-the-loop framework for a UR5e with OnRobot RG2 gripper that separates language interpretation from deterministic motion authority. A local LLM receives an ArUco-grounded scene and may propose only a predefined, schema-constrained skill. An input guard screens the utterance, a symbolic gate checks the task, and a geometric gate checks every retained trajectory sample before any controller sends; a rule-based fallback passes through the same gates. Four fixed-decoding simulation repetitions reproduced one another exactly, assessing determinism rather than independent replication. Hardware evaluation comprised one 80-row repeated-command configuration with 15 distinct texts and three 80-row sessions reusing the same 80 paraphrases across layouts. Because wording, scene, and software revision changed together, the grounding comparison is descriptive: 72/80 in A versus 163/240 in B-D. All 311 sends passed the implemented sampled geometric checks, and all 246 recorded controller-status samples were normal. Nevertheless, 14/120 must-not-move commands caused motion, including 8/45 prompt-injection trials. These geometrically certified but semantically incorrect motions show that geometric admissibility does not establish alignment with operator intent.

title: Grounding Object-to-Object Hazard Reasoning into 3D Risk Fields for Task-Conditioned Safety
abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io

title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
abstract: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.

title: Safe and Live LLM Guided UAV Navigation via Certified Corridor Feedback
venue: Innovations in Intelligent Systems and Applications Conference (ASYU)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make handy high-level planners for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), turning plain-language missions into waypoints, but their spatial reasoning is unreliable and carries no safety guarantee, so an unchecked planner can fly the vehicle straight into obstacles. A High-Order Control Barrier Function (HOCBF) safety filter stops these collisions, yet a filter that silently overrides unsafe commands trades collisions for deadlocks, because the planner keeps proposing the same blocked route and the vehicle stalls. We close the loop by reporting the filter’s correction back to the LLM in words, and the loop only helps if the message says the right thing. We test three messages of increasing control content, a number saying how hard the filter pushed back, one detour point read from the barrier gradient and our control-certified corridor, the first hops of a shortest collision-free path over the obstacle geometry, every segment checked clear before it is sent. On a real open LLM (Llama-3.3-70B) across N=30 cluttered 10-obstacle scenes, the filter removes all collisions but deadlocks 60% of runs. The number and point messages score below the filter alone (30% and 33% success versus 40%), because an unchecked detour uses up the re-planning budget. The corridor instead raises collision-free success to 73.3% with zero collisions and fewer re-plans, beating every baseline on the same scenes with no losses (McNemar p < 0.005). We also propose Feedback Conversion Efficiency (FCE), the success gained per re-plan, which measures feedback quality once safety is saturated and cleanly separates the three messages (− 2.9 −2.0, +15.2). The harness, seeds and figure code are released.

title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
abstract: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

title: Entity Graph Extraction from Legal Acts -- a Prototype for a Use Case in Policy Design Analysis
abstract: This paper presents research on a prototype developed to serve the quantitative study of public policy design. This sub-discipline of political science focuses on identifying actors, relations between them, and tools at their disposal in health, environmental, economic, and other policies. Our system aims to automate the process of gathering legal documents, annotating them with Institutional Grammar, and using hypergraphs to analyse inter-relations between crucial entities. Our system is tested against the UNESCO Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage from 2003, a legal document regulating essential aspects of international relations securing cultural heritage.

title: Automating the Analysis of Institutional Design in International Agreements
Institutional design and organised system change for sustainable urban mobility : shifting gears for transformative outcomes
abstract: This dissertation investigates how sustainability transitions in urban mobility can be effectively organised and governed to achieve transformative system change. Despite growing recognition of the transport sector’s contribution to climate change, progress towards sustainable urban mobility remains incremental. Persistent car dependence reflects institutional, political and behavioural lock-ins that constrain systemic transformation. This research is motivated by the need to better understand how organized efforts to change a system—through institutions, policies and actor interactions—can deliver transformative outcomes. The dissertation is based on three publications that collectively explore how research on sustainability transitions can facilitate more transformative change, how the institutional environment is structured to govern transitions to sustainable urban mobility and how actor interactions shape the nature, pace and outcomes of system change. To address these questions, three complementary studies were conducted. A systematic literature review (Publication I) mapped research priorities within the sustainability transitions field to evaluate their alignment with global sustainability challenges. An institutional analysis (Publication II), employing Institutional Grammar and Institutional Network Analysis, examined Finland’s multi-level governance framework regarding low-carbon mobility. A qualitative study (Publication III) combined interviews, document analysis and digital archives to trace system change in response to hype and legislative reform, examining how public–private actor interactions shape the nature, pace and outcomes of system change. The results show that transformative system change requires coherence between problem framings, institutional structures and social mechanisms. This dissertation contributes theoretically by advancing our understanding of organised system change across the problem, situational and causal realms and practically by identifying how institutions and actor interactions can be shaped to support adaptive and inclusive transitions towards sustainable urban mobility.

title: The Crisis of Imputation: From the Glass Box to the Black Box in Algorithmic Decision-Making
abstract: Modern legal orders presuppose that acts have authors: someone can be asked “why this?” and someone can answer. This paper argues that algorithmic decision-making destabilizes that institutional grammar of imputation in two coupled ways. First, it erodes agency in practice through routine delegation, converting professionals into relays of system outputs. Second, a technical shift from deterministic, inspectable procedures (“glass box”) to probabilistic, opaque learning systems (“black box”) converts legitimacy from reason-giving to performance, producing decisions that may be effective yet structurally resistant to attribution. Methodologically, the paper combines conceptual analysis, doctrinal reading of EU governance instruments (GDPR and the EU AI Act), and institutional analysis of accountability pipelines. Drawing on the triadic model of agency (initiate, judge, respond) and the ontology of signature developed in LA CAUSA PRIMERA (Fernández Tamames, 2026), it argues that explainability, while valuable, is insufficient as a remedy, and that “electronic personhood” is a liability-displacement fiction. The political remedy proposed is sovereign signing: institutionalized, reflexive human signature for high-stakes algorithmic outputs, coupled with contestability, traceability, and enforceable liability anchoring. Imputation is thereby defended as political resistance against organized irresponsibility in algorithmic governance.

title: Semyon Yakubovich: a life in Transforms. An unconventional preface for a mathematician never entirely persuaded by convention
abstract: Semyon Yakubovich: a life in Transforms. An unconventional preface for a mathematician never entirely persuaded by conventionThe story preserved in this preface begins, properly speaking, when Semyon Borisovich Yakubovich entered School Number 18 in Moscow, an institution situated, one is told, some forty-five minutes by metro from Red Square.In that city, this counts as being almost next door.Until then, his schooling in Brest, the city of his birth, first mentioned in the chronicles in 1019 and situated where the Bug and Mukhavets rivers meet, had been conventional enough.At the time, Brest belonged to the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union; Belarus as an independent state still lay in the future.His education had included French from the second year to the eighth.At School Number 18, French disappeared and English took its place.Yet the real transformation had little to do with languages.At fifteen, Semyon left home and began to live independently, a rather more demanding curriculum than any the school could formally provide.School Number 18 had been founded in 1963, in collaboration with Moscow State University, through the initiative of A. Kolmogorov and I. Kikoin.It was commonly known as FMSH-18, the characteristically economical Russian abbreviation for Physical and Mathematical School No. 18.Its full institutional title was considerably more expansive; Soviet administration had perfected the art of brevity by first producing names of heroic length and then mercifully replacing them with initials.A visit to the school's present website reveals a photograph of Kolmogorov surrounded by a group of young pupils.The reader may naturally feel invited to identify Semyon among them (Figure 1).FMSH-18 was intended for pupils of exceptional ability in mathematics, physics and chemistry.Yet it was by no means a narrowly technical institution.Semyon also remembers excellent teachers of literature and history.The scientific programme nevertheless formed its centre of gravity: approximately seven hours of mathematics each week, five of physics, together with practical classes, experiments and a kind of mathematical training that left comparatively little room for idleness.Artificial intelligence had not yet developed its present habit of appearing whenever an exercise looked even mildly inconvenient.H. G. Wells had imagined a respectable portion of the future, and I. Asimov had populated it with robots; neither, however, had thought to provide Soviet schoolchildren with one for their evening problem sets.Problems therefore had to be solved with paper, pencil, compass, memory and stubbornness, the last of these being perhaps the most important item of equipment.The principle behind the school was clear and, for its time, unusually serious: talented pupils from villages, provincial towns and the more distant reaches of the Soviet Union should not be condemned by geography.Moscow possessed advantages; the school had

title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
abstract: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

title: Beyond Modern Dualisms: Reconstructing Techno-Theology Through Animism and Divine Ethics
abstract: Techno-theology is reconsidered from a standpoint beyond modern dualisms (spirit/matter; human/nonhuman), asking how contemporary technologies come to mediate ultimate concern and thereby reconfigure meaning, agency, and moral responsibility. The article argues that techno-theology is not a new religious movement but an analytic lens for tracing the mutual mediation between technological systems and theological imaginaries. It shows, first, how technologies increasingly function as carriers of ultimacy, reorganizing authority, hope, and moral expectation. Second, it diagnoses a recurrent modern impasse: even where crude dualisms are rejected, responsibility is practically redistributed across sociotechnical arrangements in ways that diffuse accountability. Third, it proposes “divine ethics” as a minimal evaluative grammar for distinguishing idolatrous re-enchantment (salvation-by-escalation) from relational re-enchantment (limits, accountability, care). Divine ethics is operationalized through three constraints—capacity–responsibility alignment, precaution under irreversible and intergenerational risk, and future-oriented institutionalization—prioritizing prevention over post hoc blame.

title: A Review of Emission Reduction Policy Text Analysis under the Dual Carbon Context
abstract: Under the "Dual Carbon" context, China has issued a series of energy-saving, emission reduction, and low-carbon policies. These policies contain a wealth of valuable information, and many scholars have conducted research on the textual content of these policies. This article reviews the current state of research on emission reduction and related policy texts from the perspective of policy text analysis methods, providing references for relevant analyses and studies. Based on different analytical approaches to policy texts, the methods are categorized into qualitative and quantitative approaches. Given that qualitative methods are less frequently employed in this type of policy text analysis, they will not be elaborated upon. The quantitative methods are divided into policy measurement analysis, content analysis, and keyword analysis. A review of the relevant li-ter-ature introduces the characteristics of each method and their applications in emission reduction policy texts. The study finds that quantitative methods are more widely used in the analysis of emission reduction policy texts, with con-tent analysis being the most common, while keyword analysis is gradually gaining traction. Most studies emphasize the combination of methods. Future research could focus on the construction of corpora in the low-carbon policy field, better integration of Python data analysis libraries, and the design and development of specialized or general policy text analysis tools.

title: Mapping Research Paradigms in Industry–Education Integration Studies: A Bibliometric and Conceptual Review
venue: Integration of Industry and Education Journal
abstract: The accelerating convergence of artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and workforce transformation has propelled industry–education integration to the forefront of global policy agendas. Yet the intellectual structure underpinning this burgeoning research domain remains fragmented and inadequately mapped. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric and conceptual review of industry–education integration research published between 2000 and 2025, drawing upon 4,872 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases. Employing co-citation network analysis, keyword co-occurrence mapping, and thematic cluster identification through VOSviewer and CiteSpace, we systematically reconstruct the intellectual architecture of the field. The analysis reveals six distinct research paradigms that have sequentially dominated the discourse: (1) the Human Capital Formation Paradigm, rooted in neoclassical economics; (2) the Triple Helix Innovation Paradigm, emphasizing university–industry–government triadic dynamics; (3) the Regional Innovation System Paradigm, foregrounding spatial agglomeration and proximity effects; (4) the Skills Ecosystem Paradigm, advancing holistic workforce development frameworks; (5) the Platform Economy Paradigm, interrogating digital intermediation of educational labor markets; and (6) the emerging AI-Driven Workforce Formation Paradigm, conceptualizing algorithmic governance of skill supply chains. For each paradigm, we trace its theoretical genealogy, identify foundational texts, map citation networks, and evaluate explanatory scope. We further propose an integrative conceptual model—the Paradigm Convergence Framework (PCF)—that synthesizes insights across these six traditions to address the multi-dimensional challenges of AI-era industry–education coupling. The PCF positions data infrastructure, algorithmic curriculum optimization, and institutional translation capacity as the three pillars of next-generation integration architectures. This review contributes a definitive intellectual roadmap for researchers, policymakers, and institutional designers navigating the rapidly evolving landscape of industry–education integration, while simultaneously establishing a structured future research agenda organized around ten priority directions for the forthcoming decade.

title: Collaboration among Adversaries: Distributed Workflow Execution on a Blockchain
venue: Research at the University of Copenhagen (University of Copenhagen)

title: Analyzing the Thematic Evolution of Policy Design Research
venue: Revista Brasileira de Informação Bibliográfica em Ciências Sociais
abstract: The field of policy design (PD) has received increasing attention over the last few decades. During this period, the PD contributed to expanding knowledge regarding the functioning of public policies, the implementation instruments, and social effects. This review presents the PD thematic evolution through the systematization of the extant literature and grouping scientific knowledge. Our research question is: how the policy design field has evolved? The main contributions are twofold: i) quantify the research field and describe its main outputs and evolution; and ii) identify the past and the current trends and propose future avenues for research. To do so, we mapped the academic literature drawing on a systematic approach of 184 selected papers. Then, we analyzed the data by conducting a two-level analysis. We noticed that production is geographically uneven; the field has developed alongside technological evolution and adopts contemporary tools and instruments.

title: Normative Analysis of Foreign Medical and Health Worker Policies in Indonesia and Their Impact on the National Health System
abstract: This study examines the coherence and policy rationale of Indonesia’s utilization of foreign medical and health personnel (FMHP) under Government Regulation No. 28 of 2024 within the framework of the National Health System (NHS). The analysis focuses on the role of this policy as a transitional instrument to address priority referral service gaps while strengthening national health workforce capacity. Key concepts include health system governance, credentialing and clinical privileging, patient safety, informed consent, and the WHO health system building blocks. Employing a normative juridical (doctrinal legal research) method, this study applies statutory, conceptual, and systemic approaches. The scope of analysis covers health legislation, cross-sectoral labor and immigration regulations, and strategic NHS policy documents. Legal norms are examined through grammatical, systematic, and teleological reasoning and mapped against NHS output and outcome indicators. The findings demonstrate that, at the normative level, the FMHP policy is coherently designed in line with global health governance principles and oriented toward patient protection and capacity building. Nonetheless, implementation challenges persist, particularly regarding regional disparities in institutional capacity, inconsistent credentialing practices, cross-cultural communication barriers, and the absence of measurable indicators for technology transfer. The study recommends strengthening operational governance through the Deficit–Impact–Duration framework and a Technology Transfer Scorecard to ensure evidence-based evaluation. This research advances health law scholarship by integrating normative legal analysis with health system performance frameworks and proposing practical evaluative tools for assessing foreign health workforce policies as instruments of sustainable national capacity building.

title: Dual-Use Risk Governance for AI-Enabled Bioinformatics: Access Control, Publication Norms, and Responsible Capability Release
abstract: AI-enabled bioinformatics accelerates discovery by improving sequence analysis, protein modeling, and biological data integration, yet the same capabilities can be dual-use: they may lower barriers to harmful applications, amplify misuse through automation, or enable unintended escalation via rapid dissemination. This manuscript develops a publisher-ready governance framework for managing dual-use risk without disabling legitimate research. The central argument is that dual-use governance must be treated as an evidence-based lifecycle discipline—spanning research design under uncertainty, statistical explanation and causal reasoning about risk pathways, trustworthy prediction for monitoring and access decisions, and reproducible engineering practices that support audit and accountability. Across five chapters, the book formalizes risk decomposition (capability, access, intent, and context), proposes publication and release norms that preserve scientific integrity while controlling hazard-relevant details, and designs operational architectures for access control, logging, and incident response. The framework yields concrete outputs: assumption registries for risk claims, sensitivity and robustness protocols for governance decisions, monitoring covenants for capability drift, and policy instruments for cross-border coordination. Examples are globally grounded, adapting to institutional capacity differences across South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas while maintaining a consistent standard: responsible capability release requires traceable evidence, proportional controls, and revisable commitments. Keywords dual-use governance, AI bioinformatics, responsible disclosure, access control, capability release, publication norms, model cards, auditability, risk assessment, uncertainty quantification, sensitivity analysis, robustness testing, monitoring covenants, insider risk, misuse prevention, data governance, reproducibility, policy coordination, safety-by-design, accountability

title: Governing Privacy as Contexts Overlap during Crisis
abstract: Technical solutions to social problems require contextually appropriate and responsive governance. As ICTs were adopted and adapted to meet social needs, supporting social distancing, and automating services and interactions throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, associated governance often lagged, especially pertaining to privacy. Further, ICT use under these emergency circumstances raised unique challenges associated with crisis contexts, and highlighted the gaps, failures, and limitations of existing contextual privacy regulations. This chapter approaches these challenges, exploring the sociotechnical nature of governance assemblages regarding privacy, as experienced in education, through healthcare, and by labor.

title: Contextual Integrity in Large Language Models: A Review
abstract: The rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, enabling their application in diverse domains such as conversational agents and decision-support systems in sensitive areas like healthcare, finance, and eldercare. However, as LLMs are increasingly integrated into real-world contexts, concerns about their adherence to ethical principles, privacy norms, and contextual expectations have become critical. Privacy preservation is particularly pressing in interactions involving personal or sensitive data, where ensuring that LLMs align with societal norms while mitigating risks of information leakage is essential to fostering trust and ensuring responsible deployment. Contextual integrity (CI) provides a robust framework to address these challenges, emphasizing that information flows should adhere to context-specific social norms. This principle is especially vital in sensitive applications, where LLMs must evaluate roles, information attributes, and transmission principles to maintain ethical behavior. Despite their linguistic proficiency, LLMs often fail to recognize and adapt to nuanced contextual norms, a limitation exacerbated by their probabilistic nature and the biases in their training data, which can lead to inappropriate or harmful outputs. Addressing these shortcomings requires rigorous evaluation methodologies and fine-tuning strategies that embed societal and contextual norms into the models.

title: AI Risk Intelligence for Antimicrobial Resistance: A Policy-to-Implementation Blueprint for Stewardship and Biosecurity
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a slow-burning biosecurity threat that emerges from routine clinical and agricultural decisions, amplified by surveillance gaps, unequal access to diagnostics, and fragmented stewardship governance. AI risk intelligence can help identify emerging resistance patterns, forecast treatment failure risk, and target stewardship interventions, yet it also introduces new risks of overclaiming, biased allocation, privacy harms, and operational brittleness when deployed across heterogeneous settings. This manuscript develops a policy-to-implementation blueprint for AMR risk intelligence that treats analytics as a governed capability: claims are bounded by explicit assumptions, evaluated through robustness and sensitivity protocols, and monitored for drift and harm. Across five chapters, the book integrates foundations and research design under uncertainty; statistical modeling for explanation and causal inference about stewardship interventions; machine learning for prediction, generalization, and trustworthiness; big-data engineering for reproducible surveillance and MLOps-style operations; and applied sectoral playbooks spanning hospitals, communities, agriculture, and cross-border coordination. The research outputs are operational and audit-ready: AMR risk registers, evaluation covenants, monitoring charters, data governance templates, and decision tools for policymakers and implementers across South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas. Keywords antimicrobial resistance, AI risk intelligence, stewardship governance, biosecurity, surveillance systems, causal inference, robust evaluation, sensitivity analysis, prediction and calibration, distribution shift, trustworthy machine learning, diagnostic pathways, privacy and confidentiality, health equity, One Health, reproducibility, MLOps, auditability, policy implementation, cross-border coordination

title: Unravelling the Secret Language of Drivers: A Human-Centric Approach Towards Implicit Communication of Intention
abstract: This research examines human-human cooperation during the driving task to inform the design of automated vehicle (AV) human-machine interactions. It investigates how passengers intuitively infer drivers' intentions through body language and contextual cues, bypassing explicit communication. A mixed-method study introduced the "Driving Intention Grammar" (DiG), which defines key cues, sources, and sequences shaping passenger understanding. These insights informed the Intention Awareness (IA) Model, extending Endsley’s Situation Awareness framework to guide human-machine interface (HMI) design. The findings provide a foundation for anthropomorphic, context-aware, and multimodal HMIs, aiming to enhance AV transparency, predictability, and trust.

title: The value sensitive design of a preventive health check app
abstract: In projects concerning big data, ethical questions need to be answered during the design process. In this paper the Value Sensitive Design method is applied in the context of data-driven health services aimed at disease prevention. It shows how Value Sensitive Design, with the use of a moral dialogue and an ethical matrix, can support the identification and operationalization of moral values that are at stake in the design of such services. It also shows that using this method can support meeting the requirements of the General Data Protection Regulation.

title: From Technical Capability to Institutional Authority: Human Responsibility Before AI Execution
abstract: Artificial intelligence governance often treats permission as though it completes the problem of authority. Yet a system may be technically capable of acting, connected to operational resources, and supported by an earlier approval while the proposed action is no longer institutionally legitimate when execution occurs. This article distinguishes technical capability, authorization, legitimacy, and execution admissibility. It argues that consequential AI-enabled action requires more than access or prior approval: it requires valid institutional authority, identifiable decision ownership, sufficient and current evidence, applicable policy conditions, and a genuine capacity for human intervention. The article names the interval between prior authorization and present execution the execution gap. It then develops the execution gate as an institutional mechanism through which an action may be allowed, held, denied, or escalated before technical capacity becomes real-world consequence. Human responsibility, on this account, must be constituted before action, not reconstructed only after harm.

title: A Conceptual Framework for AI-Driven Industry--Education Integration
venue: Integration of Industry and Education Journal
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping production systems, organizational routines, and occupational skill profiles. Under these conditions, industry--education integration can no longer be understood as a loose arrangement of internships, guest lectures, or episodic school--enterprise cooperation. It must evolve into a dynamic, data-informed, and ethically governed ecosystem in which educational institutions and industrial actors co-design talent standards, co-produce learning resources, and co-evaluate outcomes. This article develops a conceptual framework for AI-driven industry--education integration from the perspectives of capability formation, knowledge co-creation, platform coordination, and governance. Drawing on theories of constructive alignment, experiential learning, organizational knowledge creation, activity theory, and triple-helix collaboration, the framework positions AI not as a substitute for teachers or workplace mentors, but as a mediating infrastructure that connects labour-market intelligence, curriculum reform, authentic practice, assessment, and continuous improvement. The article proposes five interdependent dimensions: strategic alignment, data and intelligence infrastructure, curriculum and pedagogy, practice and innovation ecology, and governance and ethics. It then explains four operating mechanisms through which the framework functions: dynamic skills sensing, personalized capability development, project-based knowledge circulation, and feedback-enabled institutional adaptation. On this basis, the article outlines a staged implementation path for universities and vocational institutions and develops an evaluation matrix that links learner growth, enterprise value, institutional transformation, and social inclusion. The study argues that AI-driven integration is most effective when it remains human-centered, problem-oriented, and publicly accountable. Its long-term value lies in building adaptive institutions that can respond to technological change while preserving educational depth, equity, and professional judgment.

title: From Babel to Nehemiah: A Theological Reading of Magnifica Humanitas and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This study reads the encyclical within its own theological context and questions what vision of systemic governance is implied in its argument. This reading is organized through the Systems Shift heuristic a seven-element framework drawn from socio-technical transition theory, leverage point analysis, lock-in studies, Responsible AI research, and AI governance literature but this framework serves to support the encyclical's argument, not to organize it. The study's central argument is that Magnifica Humanitas opposes two competing civilizational scripts. Babel names a social order dominated by concentrated technical power, the idolatry of profit, homogenization, and the functional reduction of human beings to data and performance. Nehemiah names the opposite order: patient reconstruction, distributed responsibility, prayerful wisdom, and the protection of the vulnerable. Leo XIV himself framed the AI ??era through these biblical images, and this paper shows that this framing carries the full weight of the encyclical’s theological anthropology: the measure of the technological order is the Incarnation the Word made flesh who reveals the human person as irreducibly embodied, relational, free, and called to communion. Five new theological dimensions are developed and integrated: (1) Trinitarian communion as the theological foundation of the Nehemiah paradigm; (2) structural sin as the proper theological name for the Babel configuration; (3) pneumatology as the basis of shared understanding; (4) incarnational biology as a deepening of Christological anthropology against AI reductionism; and (5) Marian eschatology the grammar of the Magnificat as the encyclical’s concluding horizon for the human city.

title: The embodied ethics alignment problem of AI
abstract: The problem of aligning artificial intelligence with human values is typically framed as a technical challenge: how to specify, learn, or constrain machine behavior so that artificial systems reliably produce ethically acceptable outcomes. This paper argues that this framing is fundamentally incomplete and omits an important aspect of moral agency. The central claim of this contribution is that ethics is not primarily a formalizable rule-set, preference ordering, or optimization target, but an emergent property of the human condition. Human moral agency arises from embodiment, affect, vulnerability, social embeddedness, teleological orientation, and the developmental formation of character. Alignment research, by contrast, usually treats ethics and moral agency as if it could be abstracted from these conditions and translated into reward functions, constraints, preference models, or oversight procedures. To capture this diagnosis, the paper introduces the concept of the Embodied Ethics Alignment Problem (EEAP): if moral agency depends on the embodied, affective, social, and teleological aspects of the human condition, then systems that lack those aspects cannot be ethically aligned in the “strong sense” often implied by the alignment discourse. They may be behaviorally steered toward acceptable outcomes (in the “weak sense”), but that is not the same as sharing or instantiating human moral agency. Furthermore, due to the EEAP, artificial agents may face a hard limit in terms of simulation capabilities of embodied ethics. The paper, therefore, argues that the primary task is, therefore, not to build moral machines, but to govern non-moral optimization systems within human institutions capable of bearing ethical responsibility.

title: Building a Common Language for Generative Value Creation among Heterogeneous Subjects: Insights from International Law
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Common normative languages enable coordinated action among participants whose histories, interpretive capacities, practical relations, and valuations differ. Their emergence also raises a question of authority: how can recurrent practices become shared standards without allowing those who define admissible claims and values to monopolize the conditions of cooperation? This discussion develops a generative-relational (GR) framework connecting distributed coordination, normative recognition, institutional authority, and the creation and circulation of value. It distinguishes Type II heterogeneity within human relations from Type I heterogeneity across categories of participants, including humans, artificial agents, nonhuman animals, and Earth-system processes, while suspending conclusions about their ultimate nature or moral standing. Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice supplies a domain-specific comparison for identifying legal norms; evolutionary coordination, interactive justice, polycentric governance, and generative justice supply further, non-equivalent resources. The analysis separates recurrent regularity, normative obligation, legal validity, and ethical legitimacy, and examines how control over evidential, representative, and value-conversion interfaces can reproduce meta-power. A provisional comparative framework evaluates viability, generativity, and justice separately while tracing the effects of normative arrangements on future capacities for participation and revision. The framework identifies research questions for governance involving cross-category participants and responsible normative transformation under causal uncertainty; its hypothetical cases remain conceptual stress tests.

title: Rewriting the Grammar of Schooling. Children's Imaginaries, and the School as a Learning Hub in Peripheral Contexts
venue: International Journal of Digital Literacy and Digital Competence
abstract: This article examines the transformation of schooling through the lens of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) scenario of viewing schools as learning hubs and focuses on small schools in peripheral contexts. Building on the theoretical framework of the grammar of schooling and the concept of forme scolaire, the study explores how this emerging model is interpreted through children's perspectives. Drawing on imagination laboratories conducted in three Italian schools, the research combines dialogic sessions and visual methods to investigate how students understand and reimagine the future of school. The findings show that children do not conceive of the learning hub as a purely organizational or policy model but as a reconfiguration of school spaces, learning experiences, relationships, and participation. The study contributes to the international debate by highlighting how student voice and imagination can inform the redefinition of schooling in times of structural transformation.

title: Root Metaphors of Education: Validation, Credentialism, and Digital Intelligence as an Emerging Hypothesis
abstract: This article develops a critical genealogy of three historically significant educational metaphors–literacy, schooling, and credentialism–in order to examine how different regimes of validation have organized the public recognition of learning, competence, and educational belonging. Drawing on Stephen C. Pepper, the root metaphor is understood as a matrix of intelligibility; through Ivan Illich, this notion is shifted to the historical-institutional plane, where tools, documents, schools, and credentials structure forms of authority and dependence. The article argues that literacy linked legitimate knowledge to written culture, schooling associated recognized learning with institutional trajectories, and credentialism condensed educational trajectories into diplomas, certificates, and qualifications. It then analyzes the contemporary fissure of this regime in light of micro-credentials, verifiable digital credentials, recognition of prior learning, and digital infrastructures of validation. In this context, digital intelligence is examined as a candidate for a new root metaphor. The article concludes that its philosophical-educational challenge is not merely technical, but normative and democratic.

title: Norm Formation among Heterogeneous Generative-Relational Subjects: An Evolutionary Inquiry
abstract: Norm formation among heterogeneous generative-relational systems raises a problem of interaction when participants possess different capacities, histories, practical expectations, and means of interpreting one another. An initial act of contact already relies upon a local practice, while subsequent encounters may change the very conditions under which behavior is perceived as appropriate, obligatory, or meaningful. This preliminary inquiry examines that problem through an evolutionary approach to normative interaction. Drawing on established research on conventions, social expectations, animal normativity, and multi-agent systems, it distinguishes recurrent behavior, provisional practical commitments, shared rules, normative endorsement, and legitimacy. The proposed research program considers normative initialization, provisional anchoring, partial translation, reciprocal revision, asymmetric power, and stable pluralism alongside convergence and conflict. Its generative-relational orientation permits interaction rules and interpretive capacities to change without presuming a common fitness measure or a fundamental temporal order. The manuscript develops a conceptual framework and outlines conditional formal and empirical investigations. It claims neither a general law of cross-system norm formation nor a common moral standard among human, nonhuman, artificial, and hypothetical extraterrestrial participants.

title: Distributed Legal Infrastructure for a Trustworthy Agentic Web
abstract: The agentic web marks a structural transition from a human-centered information network to a digital environment populated by artificial intelligence (AI) agents that perceive, decide, and act autonomously. As delegated action unfolds at machine speed, exceeds discrete moments of human judgment, and distributes decision-making across non-human actors, existing legal frameworks face growing strain, creating an urgent need for new mechanisms capable of sustaining legality in this emerging order. A trustworthy agentic web therefore depends on the infrastructuring of legality through interoperable protocols that organize identity, delegation, and accountability across systems, enabling coherent governance beyond isolated platforms. Towards this end, this article advances a distributed legal infrastructure (DLI), a governance paradigm composed of five interlocking layers: (1) self-sovereign, soulbound agent identities; (2) cognitive AI logic and constraint systems; (3) decentralized adjudication mechanisms for dispute resolution; (4) bottom-up agentic market regulation to mitigate information asymmetries and network effects, including insurance-based models; and (5) portable institutional frameworks that enable legal interoperability while preserving plural sources of authority. This reference framework contributes to emerging research on embedding legality within agentic web infrastructure, aligning distributed technical systems with accountability, contestability, and rule-of-law principles.

title: Artificial Intelligence–Based Decision Support Systems for Optimizing Healthcare Service Delivery and Resource Allocation
abstract: This book develops a rigorous framework for artificial intelligence–based decision support in healthcare service delivery, arguing that optimization becomes meaningful only when clinical need, operational flow, uncertainty, and governance are treated as a single analytical field. Across five chapters, the manuscript moves from foundational concepts and research design to explanatory statistics, causal reasoning, predictive learning, reproducible analytics engineering, and applied sectoral governance. The discussion emphasizes that resource allocation in healthcare cannot be reduced to simple efficiency maximization; it requires models that are interpretable, operationally relevant, fairness-aware, and resilient under changing demand conditions. The manuscript therefore integrates methodological reasoning with concrete research outputs, including uncertainty maps, causal evaluation templates, model governance artifacts, pipeline controls, and policy-ready deployment frameworks. Attention is given throughout to the practical realities of implementation across diverse health systems, including South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, where digital maturity, workforce constraints, regulatory expectations, and service burdens differ substantially. By linking analytic design to organizational action, the book offers researchers a structured research agenda, practitioners a disciplined approach to decision support adoption, and policymakers a governance vocabulary for evaluating AI-enabled optimization in healthcare. The result is a publisher-ready scholarly manuscript that treats AI not as an autonomous solution but as a governed instrument for improving access, capacity use, service quality, and strategic stewardship. Keywords healthcare decision support, service delivery optimization, resource allocation, patient flow analytics, causal inference, predictive modelling, machine learning governance, health systems engineering, MLOps in healthcare, operational intelligence, workforce allocation, emergency preparedness, equitable access, clinical operations, AI governance ___________

title: Algorithmic Governance and Public Value: Data-Driven Policy, Transparency, and Responsible Institutions
abstract: This manuscript develops an integrated framework for understanding how data-driven systems can enhance public value without weakening democratic legitimacy, administrative due process, or institutional trust. It treats algorithmic governance not as a narrow technical innovation but as a socio-technical arrangement in which policy design, data architecture, statistical reasoning, machine learning, organizational capacity, and oversight institutions must be jointly aligned. Across five chapters, the book examines the movement from problem formulation and uncertainty analysis to explanatory modeling, causal inference, predictive analytics, scalable data engineering, and sector-specific policy applications. The core argument is that responsible public-sector analytics require explicit assumptions, context-aware evaluation logic, reproducible workflows, and governance artifacts that make systems contestable, intelligible, and auditable. Rather than presenting automation as inherently efficient, the manuscript shows that institutional quality depends on how evidence is generated, how decisions are operationalized, how harms are anticipated, and how public agencies remain accountable across diverse legal, fiscal, and infrastructural settings. The resulting contribution is a publisher-ready synthesis for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking robust models, evaluation protocols, implementation roadmaps, and regulatory principles for governing algorithmic systems in South Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas. Keywords algorithmic governance, public value, data-driven policy, institutional transparency, responsible AI, causal inference, machine learning, policy analytics, reproducibility, MLOps, public administration, fairness, accountability, explainability, digital state capacity, comparative governance

title: Externalized Economy, Externalized Security Japan's Forced Evolution from a Security-outsourced Economic State to a Networked Stabilizer of the Western Pacific
Privacy governance not included: analysis of third parties in learning management systems
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address research gaps around third party data flows in education by investigating governance practices in higher education with respect to learning management system (LMS) ecosystems. The authors answer the following research questions: how are LMS and plugins/learning tools interoperability (LTI) governed at higher education institutions? Who is responsible for data governance activities around LMS? What is the current state of governance over LMS? What is the current state of governance over LMS plugins, LTI, etc.? What governance issues are unresolved in this domain? How are issues of privacy and governance regarding LMS and plugins/LTIs documented or communicated to the public and/or community members? Design/methodology/approach This study involved three components: (1) An online questionnaire about LMS, plugin and LTI governance practices from information technology professionals at seven universities in the USA (n = 4) and Canada (n = 3). The responses from these individuals helped us frame and design the interview schedule. (2) A review of public data from 112 universities about LMS plugin and LTI governance. Eighteen of these universities provide additional documentation, which we analyze in further depth. (3) A series of extensive interviews with 25 university data governance officers with responsibilities for LMS, plugin and/or LTI governance, representing 14 different universities. Findings The results indicate a portrait of fragmented and unobtrusive, unnoticed student information flows to third parties. From coordination problems on individual college campuses to disparate distributions of authority across campuses, as well as from significant data collection via individual LTIs to a shared problem of scope across many LTIs, the authors see that increased and intentional governance is needed to improve the state of student privacy and provide transparency in the complex environment around LMSs. Yet, the authors also see that there are logical paths forward based on successful governance and leveraging existing collaborative networks among data governance professionals in higher education. Originality/value Substantial prior work has examined issues of privacy in the education context, although little research has directly examined higher education institutions’ governance practices of LMS, plugin and LTI ecosystems. The tight integration of first and third-party tools in this ecosystem raises concerns that student data may be accessed and shared without sufficient transparency or oversight and in violation of established education privacy norms. However, these technologies and the university governance practices that could check inappropriate data handling remain under-scrutinized. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the governance practices of higher education institutions with respect to LMS ecosystems.

title: Cooperative or misaligned? A conceptual model of the relationship between language, action, and context in linguistic education
abstract: In educational settings specialized in linguistic instruction, an assumption is made of a direct and clear relationship between the utterances of the teachers, the activities of the learners, and the setting of the instruction, particularly treating instruction as a case of mechanical input-output functioning where there are instructions delivered and there are actions generated without considering the possibility of alternate or multiple outcomes. Nonetheless, the actual scene in the classroom is often much more complicated: language and action seem to work harmoniously, and just as often, they seem completely disconnected, yielding misunderstanding, disaffection, and bizarre results. This paper puts forward a new model for understanding the relationship between language, action, and context in the context of language teaching. It seeks to understand the conditions under which the phenomena come into alignment, or misalignment, as well as the reasons why it happens. The paper applies various understandings from applied linguistics, the study of classroom discourse, sociocultural theory, and psycholinguistics to propose a number of distinct patterns of alignment and cooperation, as well as various degrees of misalignment (semantic, procedural, affective, and contextual). The model does not consider language to be merely an uncritical means of conveying messages; it considers it a social activity that is understood and performed within particular contexts of organization, culture, and discourse. The paper subsequently claims that there is a tangible teaching consequence of making these patterns visible. With language–action–context considerations, reframing tasks, instructions, feedback, and assessments enables educators and curriculum developers to better predict learners’ misunderstandings, reluctance to engage, or difficulties in shifting verbal instructions to purposeful action. The article closes by offering practical suggestions concerning task design, classroom interaction, and teacher training, and sets out future directions for empirical research aimed at evaluating and fine-tuning the model put forth. In so doing, the article attempts to encourage researchers and practitioners to go beyond the “if we say it, they will do it” approach to promoting a more sophisticated grasp of the way in which teaching is transformed into learning, achieved through the complex interplay of language, action, and context. / Keywords: alignment and misalignment, classroom discourse, language–action–context, linguistic education, psycholinguistics, sociocultural theory, task design, teacher education.

title: A pragmatic and human-centered approach to promoting software accessibility: Design, education, governance
venue: Illinois Digital Environment for Access to Learning and Scholarship (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign)
abstract: In this dissertation, I explore three approaches to software accessibility: design, education, and governance. I aim to facilitate a discussion toward a pragmatic and integrated approach to accessibility. In the design chapter, I approached cancer survivors and spotlighted their lived experiences and challenges with software. A survey study, in-depth semi structured interviews, and a diary study were conducted to capture the multi faceted software experiences of cancer survivors. Cancer survivors may have multiple disabilities, including visual impairments, dexterity impairments/neuropathy, and chemo brain, which is unique to this population. These impairments led to difficulty in using software, which is a fundamental way for cancer survivors to search for health-related information and socialize with others. Based on the results, I proposed simple yet practical accessibility guidelines to accommodate the software needs of cancer survivors. For example, bulleted content, highlighting key information, and simplified User Interface (UI) designs make navigation easier for people with chemo brain. Such guidelines can be easily incorporated into software design and development practices. In the education chapter, I validated the possibility of teaching software accessibility before post-secondary education. Accessibility education was found to be limited in the high school curriculum, which is a missed opportunity to equip the next-generation software designers with the mindset of accessible design. I used a set of disability simulation games to successfully enhance the knowledge, awareness, and empathy of high school students regarding accessibility. Games and gamified approaches helped engage students in learning advanced computing concepts. In the governance chapter, I examined the status quo of governance approaches to improving software accessibility. I analyzed 39 software accessibility laws in 32 countries or regions to understand how they did well and where they fell short. One notable gap is that software accessibility laws have very few rules, degrading their enforceability. The laws are often written vaguely and are not friendly to law novices. Better laws stand out with concrete technical recommendations and fine-grained implementations, i.e., distinguishing between websites and mobile applications. In synthesizing the commonalities and differences between the three approaches to software accessibility, I argue that each approach has advantages and limitations — they ultimately complement each other. The design approach may best exercise a direct impact on software practitioners’ mindsets and practices if conveyed in an approachable manner. Yet designers may find limited incentives to follow guidelines outlined and promoted by accessibility researchers, which are not always in line with corporate priorities such as shipping products fast. The education approach can best prepare next-generation software practitioners. However, the long-term and actual effects of educational interventions are unpredictable and need further interrogation. The governance approach, in theory, has the power to force companies to comply with accessibility requirements. Yet, it barely works out in reality because of the ambiguous wording in accessibility laws and a lack of enforceability arising from scarce rules. I argue that an integrated approach combining design, education, and governance interventions should be used to address software accessibility issues and create a more inclusive software ecosystem.

title: Techno Constitutionalism Creates a Constitutional Neutrality Deficit in WTO Governance of Artificial Intelligence Risk Classification
abstract: Artificial intelligence will potentially raise the volume of global trade by 34 to 37 percent by 2040 through decreased trade costs and enhanced productivity [1]. Moreover, legislative attention to AI in terms of the number of times AI has been mentioned in legislative proceedings in 75 countries increased by ninefold since 2016 [2]. In this regard, the most challenging conflict of interests associated with regulating artificial intelligence within the context of international trade law can arise not only from trade protectionism, industrial policy, and strategic rivalry but also constitutional law. The emergence of risk-based AI governance means the transition of the regulation of algorithms from ordinary technology governance to the rights-based public ordering, during which countries will classify, prohibit, permit, audit, and control the use of algorithms not because of their preferences for one model of regulation and not because of protectionism or rivalry but due to the necessity of compliance with the constitutional obligations. Thus, there is the need for a new doctrinal concept that will be able to integrate constitutional obligations into the WTO legal regime and ensure that WTO discipline can preserve while accommodating constitutionally grounded differences in the regulations of AI. Otherwise, the issue of digital trade may become one of the sources of conflict between WTO's trade neutrality and constitutional sovereignty.

title: Value engineering for autonomous agents
venue: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
abstract: (English) The topic of this thesis is the engineering of values for autonomous agents. This is realised through the formulation, design and implementation of new functionalities for autonomous agents that enable reasoning in terms of values. In particular, we argue for the role of prescriptive norms as value-promoting mechanisms. Hence, value-driven agents should be able to autonomously determine which regulations (such as obligations, permissions or prohibitions) make the Multiagent System they inhabit better promote some values of interest. We lay the foundations of our work on Schwartz’s Theory of Basic Human Values to establish a consequential connection between values and norms, considering that norms are aligned with respect to values if the outcomes they incentivise satisfy the goals that capture the meaning of values in a particular context. Another feature of Schwartz’s theory that has been previously overlooked in the literature is the strong social dimension of values. That is, agents should be able to reason not just in terms of their own, but also of the values of others in their community. This points to Theory of Mind (i.e. the cognitive ability to perceive, interpret and reason about others in terms of their mental states) as an outstanding component of value-based reasoning. This thesis is structured around three main contributions (published in journal papers) plus their integration. The first contribution establishes the normvalue relationship as a consequential one in nature, and proposes a methodology for the automated synthesis and analysis of optimally value-aligned normative systems. The second contribution tackles the limitations of the first, and defines the Action Situation Language to systematically express a wide range of rules that may be implemented in a Multiagent System. This language is complemented by a game engine that automatically interprets interaction descriptions and builds their semantics as Extensive Form Games, which are later analysed with standard game-theoretical tools. This leads to a distribution over game outcomes, which are evaluated in terms of their desirability with respect to values. The third contribution introduces Theory of Mind-related functionalities into an existing Belief-Desire-Intention agent architecture, and combines them with abductive reasoning capabilities. The three contributions are integrated in a novel functionality that enables agents to reason about prescriptive norms in terms of dynamic values. This means that an autonomous agent can, at runtime, switch its value perspective to the one it estimates that another agent has. Such perspective-dependent value-based normative reasoning functionality, with its inherent social orientation, constitutes a novel contribution to the community of values for autonomous agents and paves the way for possible applications such as value-based negotiation over normative systems. In summary, value engineering is a principled and systematic approach to computational ethics, which provides an innovative tool set for integrating ethical values into the design of autonomous agents. (Català) El tema d’aquesta tesi és l’enginyeria de valors per a agents autònoms, aconseguida mitjançant la formulació, disseny i implementació de noves funcionalitats que permeten a agents autònoms raonar en termes de valors. En particular, defensem el paper de les normes prescriptives com a mecanismes de promoció de valors. Aleshores, els agents impulsats per valors deuen poder determinar de forma autònoma quines regulacions (com ara obligacions, permisos o prohibicions) promouen millor alguns valors d’interès en el Sistema Multiagent que habiten. Fonamentem el nostre treball a la Teoria de Schwartz de Valors Humans Bàsics per establir una connexió entre valors i normes basada en conseqüències, considerant que les normes estan alineades respecte als valors si els resultats que incentiven satisfan les metes que capten el significat d’aquests valors en un context determinat. Una altra característica de la teoria de Schwartz que ha estat passada per alt prèviament a la literatura és la forta dimensió social dels valors. És a dir, els agents haurien de poder raonar, no només en termes dels seus propis valors, sinó també dels d’altres a la seva comunitat. Això apunta a la Teoria de la Ment (és a dir, la capacitat cognitiva de percebre, interpretar i raonar sobre els altres en termes dels seus estats mentals) com un component destacat del raonament basat en valors. Aquesta tesi s’estructura al voltant de tres contribucions principals (publicades en revistes acadèmiques), a més de la seva integració. La primera contribució estableix la relació entre normes i valors mitjançant conseqüències, i proposa una metodologia per a la síntesi i anàlisi automatitzada de sistemes normatius òptimament alineats amb valors.
